chief_complaint: cough lasting 2 weeks following cold, clear chest X-ray
hpi_details: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with cough lasting 2 weeks following cold, clear chest x-ray. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks the cold she caught two weeks ago never fully cleared up and left her windpipe raw and irritated.
concerns: She is worried that a cough lasting this long means she is developing chronic asthma or permanent damage in her airways.
expectations: She hopes to hear reassuring confirmation that her lungs are clear and receive medicine to stop the nighttime coughing so she can sleep.

available_results.value: Clear lungs without focal air-space opacity, pleural effusion, or pneumothorax

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Bronchitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Most uncomplicated acute bronchitis is self-limited; management emphasizes symptom support, clear safety-netting, and avoiding unnecessary antibiotics.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: cough lasting 2 weeks following cold, clear chest X-ray

Key HPI features: A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic with cough lasting 2 weeks following cold, clear chest x-ray. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Acute Bronchitis.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Bronchitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Pneumonia without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe hypoxemia (SpO2 < 90%).
management_principles: Rule out pneumonia or other serious illness using vital signs and examination, then provide symptom support and avoid routine antibiotics
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient has a 2-week cough after a cold, with a reported clear chest X-ray and fatigue. A viral trigger is plausible but not proven.
reference_soap.objective: Obtain full vital signs including oxygen saturation and a focused respiratory examination; reassess for pneumonia if there are abnormal vital signs or focal lung findings.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute cough illness, most consistent with uncomplicated acute bronchitis after assessment excludes pneumonia and other important alternatives.
reference_soap.plan: Explain that post-viral cough can persist for several weeks. Encourage fluids and discuss limited-evidence symptomatic options after checking contraindications; do not routinely prescribe antibiotics. Give explicit return precautions for hypoxaemia, significant dyspnoea, chest pain, confusion, persistent high fever, haemoptysis, or deterioration. Re-evaluate a prolonged or worsening cough for pneumonia, asthma, pertussis when clinically suggested, or other causes.

must_ask.objective: Preceding cold symptoms and cough duration
must_ask.say: Did this cough start after a cold, and how many days has it been going on?
Are you coughing up any phlegm, and if so what colour is it?

must_ask.objective: Fever and systemic symptom screen to exclude pneumonia
must_ask.say: Have you had any fever, chills, or felt short of breath?
Your chest X-ray came back clear - has anyone explained what that means for your treatment?

must_ask.objective: Smoking status and history of wheeze or asthma
must_ask.say: Do you smoke, and have you ever been told you have asthma or wheeze easily?

history.answer: I caught a cold about two weeks ago, and while the other cold symptoms went away, this hacking cough just won't stop.
It has been going on for exactly two weeks now, and it has actually felt a bit more nagging over the last few days.
It started with a runny nose, mild sore throat, and feeling run-down two weeks ago. Those symptoms resolved within four or five days, but the cough remained.
It was mostly dry at first, but lately I cough up small amounts of thin, whitish phlegm. There is no foul smell or thick yellowish-green mucus.
I cough throughout the day, but it tends to get worse at night when I lie down to sleep. Lying flat doesn't suffocate me, but my throat tickles more.
No, I don't have severe coughing fits that make me gasp for air with a whoop, and I haven't vomited from coughing.
Cold outdoor air and dry rooms definitely trigger the coughing tickle. Drinking warm water seems to soothe my throat temporarily.
No, I haven't heard any whistling or wheezing in my chest, and I don't get out of breath walking up stairs.
I had a mild fever for the first couple of days of the cold, but I have not had any fever or chills since then.
I feel worn out and tired, but I think that's mostly because the cough keeps waking me up at night.
No, I have never seen any blood or pink streaks in my phlegm.
No, my weight has been completely steady and I haven't had any drenching night sweats.
I feel some mild muscle soreness across the center of my chest from coughing so hard, but no sharp stabbing pain when I breathe in.
My runny nose and stuffiness cleared up about ten days ago. I don't feel mucus dripping down the back of my throat anymore.
No, I don't experience heartburn, acid regurgitation, or sour fluid backing up into my mouth.
No, I can sleep flat without needing extra pillows, and my legs and ankles haven't swollen.
No, I do not take any blood pressure pills, ACE inhibitors, or regular medications.
No, I have never had tuberculosis, and to my knowledge, I haven't had contact with anyone who had it.
A couple of my coworkers had mild colds around the time mine started, but nobody had a severe or persistent lung infection.
I work in a standard office setting, so I'm not exposed to chemical fumes, industrial dust, birds, or mold.
No, I don't have a history of asthma, allergic rhinitis, or eczema, and I didn't wheeze as a child.
I had a chest X-ray taken at a clinic two days ago, and the doctor told me that my lungs looked completely clear.
I thought the head cold I had two weeks ago just lingered and left my bronchial tubes raw and irritated.
I'm worried that having this cough linger for two whole weeks means I'm developing asthma or permanent lung damage.
I'm hoping to hear that my lungs sound clear and get something to stop the coughing at night so I can finally sleep.
I have no chronic medical conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, or heart trouble.
I have never had any surgeries, and I have never been admitted to a hospital.
I took some over-the-counter cold medicine during the first few days, but I am not taking anything right now.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or environmental triggers.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes.
I only drink alcohol socially, perhaps one or two glasses of beer once a month.
I work as an office administrative assistant and live in an apartment with my husband.
There is no family history of chronic cough, asthma, or lung malignancies.
My last menstrual period started exactly two weeks ago, and my menstrual cycles are regular every 28 days.
We use condoms consistently for contraception, and there is no chance that I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Alert, comfortable at rest, coughing intermittently, in no acute respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, body temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.
Mild pharyngeal erythema without exudate; nasal mucosa pink without purulent drainage or cobblestoning.
No tenderness on palpation or percussion over the frontal and maxillary sinuses bilaterally.
No cervical, submandibular, or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy palpable.
Symmetric chest expansion with equal tactile fremitus bilaterally and no chest wall tenderness.
Resonant percussion notes throughout all lung fields bilaterally with no areas of dullness.
Clear vesicular breath sounds throughout bilateral lung fields with no crackles, wheezes, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
No pretibial pitting edema bilaterally, and no digital clubbing or cyanosis.
